historyReviewBoundary: All 115 histories have author source checks. Final independent review covered metadata and numerical checks for all 115 classes, 12 deeper class targets and source-gap samples in seven classes. It did not independently verify every passage of every cited source.

history.name: GLP-1 receptor agonists

starting.description: Gut-hormone/incretin physiology and the insulin-stimulating activity of processed endogenous GLP-1 supplied the biological starting point. A separate exendin-4 natural-peptide branch later supplied another receptor agonist lead. The class developed from observed biological signals rather than inventing the action from scratch.

inspiration.description: Incretin physiology, endogenous processed GLP-1, and the distinct natural exendin-4 branch. The final chemical/protein engineering retains the observation-led origin.

steps.description: Proglucagon supplies GLP-1 sequences. Investigation of their processed forms provided an endogenous peptide hypothesis rather than merely a receptor target.
In 1987, synthetic GLP-I(7-37), unlike GLP-I(1-37), stimulated insulin secretion in perfused rat pancreas. Later patient infusion experiments lowered glucose and supported GLP-1 therapy.
A distinct natural-product branch followed exendin-3: Eng and colleagues searched H. suspectum venom and isolated exendin-4, subsequently used as the exenatide template.

Exendin-4 was reproduced synthetically as exenatide. Human GLP-1 was separately adapted by fatty-acid derivatization for albumin binding; semaglutide added position-8 stabilization and optimized the fatty di-acid/linker. Dulaglutide represents Fc fusion for prolonged exposure.
Exenatide entered the market in 2005. The human-GLP-1 branch yielded liraglutide and later long-acting members, preserving its endogenous ancestry alongside the separate exendin branch.

design.description: Synthetic peptide experiments established activity; subsequent acylation, non-natural residue substitution and protein fusion extended exposure and stability while preserving GLP-1 receptor agonism. Semaglutide and dulaglutide use the human-GLP-1 branch; exenatide is a synthetic replica of the separate exendin-4 lead.

circumstances.description: The cited hormone-analogue engineering and targeted exendin search were deliberate. An accidental class-opening discovery is not established by the selected accounts.

limits: The class has multiple observation-led branches; that alone does not make its discovery basis mixed.
Semaglutide and dulaglutide belong to the human GLP-1 branch, not the lizard exendin lineage.
This bounded example does not adjudicate sole-discoverer credit or cover dual GIP/GLP-1 agonists or DPP-4 inhibitors.
A synthetic experimental replica is not a design-from-scratch origin; later rational optimization remains part of the observation-led development chain.
conflicts: Holst 2019 describes the exendin-4 isolation material as saliva rather than venom. Eng 1992's original title and abstract explicitly report venom; Knudsen/Lau also use venom. This record follows the original report's wording and preserves the discrepancy without treating it as a different molecular lineage.
gaps: Eng 1992 was read at abstract extent only. The full Mojsov 1987 original was read, but early human infusion reports and individual dulaglutide engineering reports were not independently reopened; those links rest on the explicitly identified retrospective sections.

humanContributionInterpretation.summary: Effective GLP-1 treatment in humans was limited by rapid disappearance and short action; this motivated longer-acting analogues and exposure-extension strategies.
humanContributionInterpretation.scope: Human clinical pharmacology and refinement qualify; this does not recast the initial peptide isolation or all incretin work as noninterventional observation.
